The next most efficient step to evaluate this is an imaging study of the chest to look for a pulmonary mass, lymphadenopathy, or metastases. A contrast-enhanced chest CT is more sensitive and specific than a chest X-ray and will better guide further workup.

[TEST] Order contrast-enhanced CT scan of the chest (CT chest with IV contrast).

The next essential initial test is a CBC with differential and peripheral smear to look for leukocytosis/lymphocytosis, anemia, thrombocytopenia, or circulating malignant cells that would point toward leukemia/lymphoma and guide urgent further testing.

[TEST] Order CBC with differential and peripheral blood smear.

[THOUGHT] The patient has months of fatigue and marked unintentional weight loss, generalized lymphadenopathy, splenomegaly, lymphocytosis on CBC, and flow cytometry showing a monoclonal B-cell population with a phenotype consistent with CLL/SLL. The combination of peripheral blood lymphocytosis plus the immunophenotype (monoclonal CD5+ CD19+ B cells typical on flow cytometry) and splenomegaly makes chronic lymphocytic leukemia the most likely diagnosis rather than isolated lymph node–predominant SLL.

[DIAGNOSIS] Chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL).
